chapters.summary: Gennaro identifies himself as chair and announces an oversight hearing on coastal resiliency along with three bills. He says the committee will hear Intros 343, 931, and 936.
chapters.title: Chair Gennaro opens hearing on coastal resiliency oversight

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me to silence my phone.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Let me do that now.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I'll just put it away.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Jim Gennaro, Chair of the Committee on Environmental Protection and Waterfronts.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Today we will hold an oversight hearing on coastal resiliency as well as the following legislation.

chapters.summary: Gennaro describes Intro 343 on waiving crane permit fees for solar installations, Intro 931 on a mobile drinking fountain program, and Intro 936 on creating a Department of Coastal Protection. He says the new department would design and deploy shoreline protection measures.
chapters.title: Gennaro summarizes solar, drinking fountain, and coastal protection bills

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Intro number 343, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse, in relation to waiving fees for street crane permits related to solar installations.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Intro 931, sponsored by Councilmember Harvey Epstein, in relation to requiring DEP to establish a mobile drinking fountain program.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Intro number 936, sponsored by myself in relation to the creation of a Department of Coastal Protection.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Which

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: would be tasked with designing and deploying measures and infrastructure to protect the city's shoreline and coast from storms, erosion, and the effects of climate change.

chapters.summary: Gennaro notes the approaching 14th anniversary of Superstorm Sandy and describes the recent nor'easter that caused coastal flooding and killed NYCHA worker Leighton Brown. He offers condolences and compares New York's flooding with worse damage in New Jersey.
chapters.title: Gennaro marks Sandy anniversary and weekend nor'easter damage

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We are just about a month away from the 14th anniversary of Superstorm Sandy.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And this past weekend, the city was hit with a nor'easter, which brought coastal flooding, strong winds, and heavy rain.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: which unfortunately led to the passing of New Yorker and NYCHA employee Leighton Brown, a maintenance supervisor who was tragically struck and killed by a falling tree during the storm.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I would like to offer my sincerest condolences to Mr.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Brown's family and friends.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: The weekend storm coincided with a full moon and high tide, and its confluence of factors led to significant coastal flooding in low-lying waterfront neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: While the city was spared the worst of these effects, our neighbors in New Jersey were not so lucky.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Across the state, the combination of severe storm surge and higher-than-average tide washed away entire stretches of beach, creating significant economic damage and undoing millions of dollars in

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: recent beach re-nourishment work.

chapters.summary: Gennaro recalls introducing the 2012 bill that became Local Law 42, codifying the NYC Panel on Climate Change and Climate Adaptation Task Force. He cites NPCC 2024 projections for sea-level rise through 2100.
chapters.title: Gennaro recounts Local Law 42 and sea-level projections

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: As some of you know, back in 2012, well, I don't think anybody knows this, but I know it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: As some of you, as you probably don't know, back in 2012, I

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: introduced the bill that would go on to become Local Law 42 of 2012, codifying the New York City Panel on Climate Change and the Climate Adaptation Task Force.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: According to...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: The panel's 2024 report, that is the NPCC, local sea levels are projected to rise between six

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: These are their projections, not mine.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: To rise between six inches.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Local sea levels are projected to rise between 6 inches and approximately 12 inches by the 2030s, 1 to 2 feet by the 2050s, and 2 to 5.5 feet by

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I think those estimates are a little high.

chapters.summary: Gennaro digresses on conflicting state sea-level estimates from Columbia and Stony Brook, arguing that two sets of books undermine public confidence in climate science. He says preparation is still necessary despite uncertainty.
chapters.title: Gennaro criticizes inconsistent sea-level rise projections

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And you're going to go off on a tangent for a minute.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And therein lies, you know, some of the people who criticize climate change and don't believe in it, don't, you know, they don't know, you know, they don't have confidence in it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Back when I was working for the state as the...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: DEP, as the DE, the state DEC deputy commissioner, we were, for our purposes in DEC, using

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: numbers for sea level projections that were projected by Columbia.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And the governor's office of storm recovery were using numbers that were generated by my alma mater,

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Stony Brook University, their department of marine, oh God, senior moment, department of

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: SOMAS, School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, they're high-end estimates for sea level rise by X date, whatever it was, or half of what the Columbia projections were.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so I raised the point.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: With the commission of DEC and state government at large, people see state government as kind of like one entity, and we have two sets of books for sea level rise.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So if you're at the governor's office of storm recovery, you're seeing the high-end estimate of like X, and if you look at Columbia's number, the high-end estimate was 2X.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We shouldn't have two sets of books, and this is why people lose confidence in climate forecasting and sea level rise projections.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Because they're like personalities of...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, the one who was doing it at Stony Brook was a, he was a Nobel laureate.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And he's very strict in terms of we don't know something until we know it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so if we don't know it, it's not going in the calculus for the projections.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We can end up, there could be things that we don't know, factors that we don't really, that we think are out there, but we haven't really studied them enough that, like, they're not going in the projection.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So we're going to be conservative.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And whereas some other entities are like, well, you have to build in a little bit of a fudge factor because nature always has something out there that we don't yet know.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So let's use the Ouija board and try to...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Fit it in somehow to account in our current projections that which we don't fully know yet.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so as a scientist, it's always like kind of annoyed me.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so that's two minutes of your life you can't get back.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Sorry, but hopefully it was enriching about climate science and why people sometimes poke at it, because that's exactly the thing people would say.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: New York State's got two sets of books on like what climate, on what sea level rise projections are.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, one of them has got to be wrong, probably both of them.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so that doesn't mean we shouldn't endeavor to figure it out.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It doesn't mean we shouldn't try to prepare for it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But these are some of the frustrations when you're dealing with people who don't want to even recognize climate change and sea level rise as a thing.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: This is fodder for them to throw in our face, and I don't like to serve up things that people are going to throw in our face.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That's three minutes you can't get back.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Where were we?

chapters.summary: Gennaro cites NPCC projections for increased annual precipitation and argues stronger storms require a city agency or bureau to holistically plan coastal response. He wants to codify the existing Bureau of Coastal Resilience.
chapters.title: Gennaro cites precipitation projections and need to codify Bureau

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: High-end estimates for annual precipitation project, and this is NPCC, project an increase of up to 10% in annual precipitation by the 2030s, 14% by the 2050s, and 30%.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Stronger and more severe storms like this one, like the one this past weekend, are likely to become increasingly common as time goes on.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We all know that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: This ongoing threat requires a city agency, or in this case, an agency bureau right there.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: To holistically plan and manage the city's response.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: At this hearing, I'm looking forward to learning about the Bureau's burgeoning role in coastal resilience so that we may codify their important work.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, it's important to understand that, you know, the Bureau that would be created through this law already exists.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It's not yet codified in law, and so we think it's important to codify it in law so that successive administrations will have no ability to

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: not continue the work of this important bureau.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I am also looking forward to hearing feedback on the other legislation so that we can ensure that these bills are the best and most effective they can be.

chapters.summary: DeFalco introduces herself as Deputy Commissioner for Public Affairs at DEP and introduces colleagues from the Bureau of Coastal Resilience and DOB. She says they will discuss coastal resilience and the bills.
chapters.title: DEP Deputy Commissioner Beth DeFalco introduces panel

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Terrific.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gennaro and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: My name is Beth DeFalco.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Public Affairs at the New York City Department of Environmental Protection.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleague, Catherine Prabilski, the Assistant Commissioner of Engineering in the Bureau of Coastal Resilience, as well as Jill Hubecki, Assistant Commissioner of Engineering Services, and Wendy Wan, Borough Commissioner of Central Development Programs from the Department of Buildings.

chapters.summary: DeFalco details storm surge, high winds, and flooding in Jamaica Bay, Howard Beach, Staten Island, City Island, and Red Hook. She notes downed trees, the death of Mr. Brown, and DEP pumping and tree removal efforts.
chapters.title: DeFalco describes weekend nor'easter impacts and DEP response

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're here today to discuss the city's coastal resilience work and then the other legislation as well before the committee.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by speaking about this past weekend's nor'easter.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The storm brought high winds, rain, and coastal storm surge, particularly in the communities surrounding Jamaica Bay, Hamilton and Howard Beach areas, and Staten Island's South Beach on City Island in my neighborhood of Red Hook.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Surging high tides overtopped the coastlines repeatedly over three days, inundating some low-lying communities.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Hundreds of trees were downed, primarily in Brooklyn and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And tragically, as you mentioned, Chair, we lost the life of a night maintenance worker, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Brown.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: As tides receded, DEP crews responded across the city to pump out low-lying areas that could not drain naturally.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: In partnership with New York City Emergency Management, we continued this response as the storm withdrew from the area on Monday.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's important to understand that pumping only works once the tides go down.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Otherwise, whatever we've pumped out is just reflooded with the high tide.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: DEP also responded to help with the removal of fallen trees.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Our forestry crews from upstate, from the watershed upstate, came down to the city to help Parks Department cut up and remove downed trees across streets and parks.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And while the storm brought significant damages from storm surge and high winds, the rainfall was moderate and steady, so we saw only very minor inland stormwater flooding.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says NYC has 520 miles of shoreline and must get ahead of risk with a coordinated citywide approach, not isolated projects. She describes DEP's 2023 creation of the Bureau of Coastal Resilience and its responsibilities.
chapters.title: DeFalco outlines need for coordinated coastal resilience

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Now to coastal resilience, which is obviously one of the reasons we're here today.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: As the weekend storm reminded us, New York City is a coastal city.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We have 520 miles of shoreline, millions of...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: New Yorkers living and working near the water, and a changing climate that is making the risks that we face more urgent.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: For too long, cities like New York have largely followed the same cycle.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: A major storm hits, we recover, we rebuild, and we move on.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But that can't be our long-term strategy.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We need to get ahead of the risk.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Just as importantly, we need a coordinated citywide approach to coastal resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Not a collection of individual projects that are planned, built, and maintained in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: For us to be successful, we need strong institutional capacity, technical capacity, and financial capacity, which must include state and federal partners and sustained political support.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That work is underway right now at DEP.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: In 2023, DEP created the Bureau of Coastal Resilience, or BCR as we often call it, to bring greater focus and accountability to this enormous challenge.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: BCR is responsible for planning the future of our coastline and for the operation and maintenance of the city's growing network of coastal flood protection infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This is truly a citywide effort.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: DEP works closely with Parks, EDC, SBS, DOB, DDC, DOT, City Planning, MOCEJ, and many other partners to move critical coastline resilience projects forward across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But DEP isn't simply building coastline resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're building the workforce, the expertise,

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: operating procedures, and the maintenance systems necessary to make sure this infrastructure actually works when New Yorkers need it.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says Mayor Mamdani committed $43.2 million to expand BCR from six to 75 employees, adding engineers, planners, field crews, and flood resilience experts. She says the city is now building and operating projects.
chapters.title: DeFalco announces $43.2M expansion of Bureau of Coastal Resilience

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Earlier this year, Mayor Momdami made a significant commitment to this work.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: $43.2 million to dramatically expand the Bureau of Coastal Resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That investment will grow the Bureau from just six employees to 75.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're adding engineers, planners, field crews, and other flood resilience experts.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That matters because the city is entering a new phase of coastal resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're no longer simply talking about what these projects could look like.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're building them.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We are operating them.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And we need to make sure that they continue protecting New Yorkers for decades to come.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Today, BCR oversees 16 active infrastructure projects in various stages of planning, design, and construction.

chapters.summary: DeFalco lists 16 active BCR projects, including Eastside Coastal Resilience, Brooklyn Bridge Montgomery, Staten Island seawall, Seaport, and Red Hook. She gives costs, lengths, and populations protected.
chapters.title: DeFalco details major coastal resilience projects

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Among the largest are the Eastside Coastal Resilience, Brooklyn Bridge Montgomery Coastal Resilience, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Army Corps'Staten Island Seawall, Seaport Coastal Resilience, and the Red Hook Coastal Resilience Project, among many others.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The Eastside Coastal Resilience Project represents a $1.46 billion investment that provides 2.4 miles of coastal protection from East 25th Street to Montgomery Street.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's designed to protect approximately 110,000 New Yorkers, including roughly 28,000 residents of public housing.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And it's designed to protect them from a 100-year coastal storm while accounting for projected sea level rise through 2050.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The Brooklyn Bridge Montgomery Coastal Resiliency Project is a $388 million project that will protect approximately 44,000 residents along a half-mile stretch between Montgomery Streets and the Brooklyn Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The South Shore of Staten Island seawall is a $2.4 billion project that will protect over 30,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Superstorm Sandy claimed the most lives of any New York City borough.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This project rebuilds the FDR boardwalk with a 5.5 mile long continuous protection.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The $228 million Seaport Coastal Resilience Project will extend protection from Brooklyn Bridge to John Street.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And in Brooklyn, the $208 million Red Hook Coaster Resiliency Project will create approximately two miles of protection along the Red Hook waterfront, including the Atlantic Basin and Beard Street, benefiting approximately 6,000 residents.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Over the next four years, these and other projects will increasingly move from plans on paper to actual infrastructure protecting New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says building infrastructure is not enough; the city must operate and maintain a new class of assets. She notes BCR assumed responsibility for 12 floodgates and 1.4 miles of flood wall from ESCR.
chapters.title: DeFalco discusses operating and maintaining new flood infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Building infrastructure is not the end of the work.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Somebody has to operate and maintain that infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And it may sound obvious, but this is an entirely new class of city asset.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So a new process has to be developed.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: In February of 2025, the Bureau of Coastal Resiliency reached an important milestone with an assumed responsibility for the first 12 floodgates and 1.4 miles of flood wall constructed as part of the Eastside Coastal Resilience Project.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: During a coastal storm, those gates can close and help protect communities from storm surge coming off the East River.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: While the overall ESCR project is not yet complete, portions already in place can be activated if necessary for hurricanes.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: As additional coastline projects are completed, BCR will assume responsibility for more of these assets.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says BCR is developing first coastal infrastructure design standards and an asset management system. It is also working toward a comprehensive vision for all 520 miles of coastline considering risk, equity, land use, and maintenance.
chapters.title: DeFalco describes design standards and comprehensive coastal vision

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: At the same time, we have to look beyond the problem.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: projects already underway.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: BCR is developing the city's first coastal infrastructure design standards and an asset management system for coastal resilience infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The Bureau is also working toward a comprehensive vision for all 520 miles of New York City's coastline, one that considers risk, equity, land use, community needs, and the realities of maintaining this infrastructure over generations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We need a plan where no one's left behind.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But infrastructure, but realistically, that's a huge challenge.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The plan needs to be responsive to the priorities of New Yorkers, taking affordability, housing, and safety into account, and we know that won't be easy.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Coastal resilience is too big and too complex for any one sector to solve alone.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's a shared challenge requiring a shared solution.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Fully protecting New York City's coastline will require investments measured in tens of billions of dollars, and we could be looking at anywhere from approximately $1 to $2 billion annually over the next 20 to 30 years.

chapters.summary: DeFalco estimates $1–$2 billion annually over 20–30 years and says the city cannot do it alone. She discusses HATS, the Army Corps, and the need for sustainable funding and government structure.
chapters.title: DeFalco says coastal protection requires billions and federal partners

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The city cannot do this alone.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Washington must continue to play a leading role.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're working with our federal and state partners on a number of projects around the city, including several mentioned here today.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We also continue to work with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Army Corps of Engineers and our state partners to advance the New York-New Jersey Harbor and Tributary Study, also known as HATS.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: In 2022, HATS identified the broader protections we need for coastal protection projects across the region with a $52 billion price tag.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But that direction must be matched with sufficient federal funding to move the projects toward construction.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Completing this work is essential to protect

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: New Yorkers over the coming decades.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The scale of hats underscores that protecting New York City from coastal flooding requires major investments across our shoreline, not just individual projects.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We need to be candid about the reality that this level of protection is ongoing and going to be expensive.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We cannot simply identify what needs to be built.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We also need a realistic plan for how to pay for it and how to pay and operate and maintain it once it's built.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: A floodgate is only useful if it works when you need it, and not just when it's shiny and new, but when the next big storm comes, whether that's tomorrow or 50 years from now.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Much of this infrastructure requires ongoing maintenance, and we must invest in protecting the assets we worked so hard to build.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: BCR is working with OMB and EDC and the Law Department and MOCEJ to examine sustainable funding and financing mechanisms, as well as the government structure necessary to manage this growing portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Getting that piece right is crucial.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says DEP shares the goal of clear accountability for coastal resilience but warns against fragmenting the existing Bureau. She asks the Council to consider strengthening rather than duplicating institutional structure.
chapters.title: DeFalco testifies on Intro 936 Department of Coastal Protection

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Now I'd like to speak about the bills that are also being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Intro 936, the Department of Coastal Protection.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This bill would establish a new Department of Coastal Protection to oversee measures and infrastructure and address the growing risks associated with coastal storms and climate change.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We appreciate the council's focus and advocacy on this issue greatly.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We share the goal behind the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: New York City needs a clear responsibility and accountability for coastal resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That is precisely why the city created and is now

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: dramatically expanding DEP's Bureau of Coastal Resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Over the past several years, we've been building the expertise, staffing partnership, and operating capacity necessary to manage this work.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: BCR is already overseeing a growing portfolio of projects, assuming responsibility for completed infrastructure, developing citywide standards, and planning for the long-term future of our coastline.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: As the council considers this legislation, we think it's important to closely look at the institutional structure already being built and make sure that any changes strengthen the city's ability to deliver this work rather than inadvertently fragmenting it.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity to continue that conversation with the council following today's hearing.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says DEP understands extreme heat concerns but warns the bill would require significant resources and pull staff from water supply duties. She points to cooling stations, park fountains, and other agency initiatives as alternatives.
chapters.title: DeFalco raises concerns with Intro 931 mobile drinking fountains

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 931 on mobile drinking fountains, this bill would require DEP to maintain a fleet of mobile drinking fountains and deploy them throughout the city when temperatures are expected to exceed 82 degrees.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We absolutely understand the concern behind this bill.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Extreme heat is dangerous and access to drinking water is an important part of the city's response.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That said, there are a number of concerns that we have with the legislation as currently written.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: DEP's first responsibility during periods of extreme heat is to make sure that New Yorkers continue to have safe, reliable drinking water coming out of their taps.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Hot weather places additional demands on our water system and our workforce, things like managing open hydrants and other water conditions.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Requiring DEP employees to simultaneously deploy, operate, and maintain a separate fleet of mobile drinking fountains would require significant additional resources and could pull personnel away from the critical water supply and infrastructure responsibilities at exactly the time that we need the most.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We believe there may be better ways to accomplish this goal of increasing access to drinking water during extreme heat.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The city's implemented a record number of cooling stations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We've got nearly 600.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: They're strategically placed around the city, providing water and air conditioning.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And there are more than 3,400 water fountains and parks around the city.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: NYSIM and DOT have been testing and launching a number of cooling initiatives, such as pop-up misting stations and installing heat adaptation measures in right-of-ways and bus shelters.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We'd be happy to work with the council and our partner agencies to expand existing cooling resources.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: resources and explore additional options.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says Intro 343 concerns crane permit fees for solar installation and that DOB manages crane permitting. She says DOB supports the intent and wants to work with Council on renewable energy legislation.
chapters.title: DeFalco defers to DOB on Intro 343 solar crane fees

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Intro 343, fees for installation of solar power and energy systems.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This bill pertains to waiving the permit fees for cranes used in connection with solar installation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We defer to DOB on this, who manages the city's crane permitting.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: DOB supports the intent of the bill and appreciates the need to incentivize property owners to install solar energy systems.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The agency looks forward to working with the council to advance legislation to facilitate the installation and use of renewable energy systems.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says NYC has made progress since Sandy but the challenge remains enormous. She says the city must ensure billions in coastal infrastructure work together and are ready for the next storm.
chapters.title: DeFalco closes DEP testimony and offers questions

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: New York City has made enormous progress since Hurricane Sandy, but the scale and challenge ahead of us is equally enormous.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We now have billions of dollars of coastal infrastructure moving from planning and design into construction and operation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Our job is to make sure those investments work together, that somebody is accountable for them, and that most importantly, they're ready when the next storm comes.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That's what we are building at DEP.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: My colleagues and I are happy to take any questions that you might have.

chapters.summary: Epstein thanks Gennaro and explains Intro 931 aims to improve public water access on hot days, especially in low-income communities. He asks whether the city can better provide publicly available water.
chapters.title: Epstein advocates for mobile drinking fountains in heat-vulnerable neighborhoods

utterances.text: I'm glad to see that you're back here with us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're doing e-bike here across the street, so I appreciate being taken out of turn.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to check in because...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Obviously, we want to have access to water, especially on hot days, especially in high heat areas in our city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Especially, you know, not just my district, but across our city, we have a lot of lower income communities where they don't have access to publicly available water fountains and water stations.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I know during different times, you know, the cities put them out.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do we do a better job making publicly available water available to New Yorkers, especially in hot days, especially in low-income communities in our city?

chapters.summary: DeFalco says DEP appreciates the advocacy but the bill poses logistical and workforce challenges, requiring two people per station and over 100 staff. She notes DEP has only nine emergency fountains and has reduced the program due to overtime costs.
chapters.title: DeFalco cites staffing and cost concerns with mobile fountain bill

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Well, Councilman, first of all, we very much appreciate your advocacy on this issue, and we're very proud of our product.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So it's not that we don't want to be out there making sure that people have no issue getting it.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That said, I think that some of the logistical problems that we see with the bill, there are large challenges in terms of cost and workforce.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So temperature aside, we...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: You need two people per station.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So you're looking at more than 100 people, more people than we would just be adding to the Bureau of Coastal Resiliency that we just mentioned, in order to be able to even staff those.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We don't have 100-plus fountains.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I mean, those are some of the logistical problems.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many fountains do we have available?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The ones that we have now that we use for emergencies, nine.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know I've seen them put out in all sorts of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So there's a capital request to getting more fountains.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that an issue?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Well, right now we use them for emergency purposes only in the last few years in terms of like water outages or water main break.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I've seen them when we do like open streets or on the street or.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We've reduced that program pretty significantly because of the overtime costs.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And also because with increased flooding, we've started to direct resources toward things like flooding town halls and other things.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: You know, we found that a lot of those, as much as we would like to be able to do that, there are other ways.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That are less resource dependent, that people can get access to water.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think during, especially heat days, more than 600 cooling stations, more than 3,400 water fountains in public parks.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The way that this bill is set up right now, we'd be millions of dollars it would cost to set this up.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But is there a way to, you know, we obviously keep talking about it, but

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's a way to narrowly tail this to ensure, like, this is my concern, and I see it in parts of my district.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: where there's just not publicly available water fountains and there aren't cooling stations that are readily available for some of our young people.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So your answer is to build more cooling stations instead of just putting out water fountains.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I would defer to NISM on the setup and the actual locations for those cooling stations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But given that you've already got people staffing,

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Those stations there already exist as they exist.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That might be one opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think that this might be something that we could talk about in terms of is this something that should be DEP's core function.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The money to pay for this would be the same money that comes from our water rate money, so money that we use for flood protection and mitigation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's probably worth talking about.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The idea is noble, whether it belongs in this agency or how it might be done in partnership with other agencies as opposed to DEP doing it by itself.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I hear your concern that maybe DEP may not be the right agency because you're not doing as much publicly facing work in this relationship where other agencies are out on the street.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Providing services to people, you know, OEM, other agencies where they're just have a publicly facing, especially during heat event, you know, events in our city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you're saying that some collaboration could be a better approach to doing it and not focusing on DEP.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that what I hear?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Yes, I think that there's another way to do it.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Our core focus, especially during heat emergencies,

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: making sure that our system is operating.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: closing hydrants, you know, making sure that those core functions and responsibilities are happening.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: In order to set these up, we'd be using people who do those operations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: You know, we don't have enough people to actually stay with the fountains by themselves.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So if they're not staffed,

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: People don't always use them as intended, we found in the past.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So that's why it might make sense to set it up differently than to just have standalone temporary moving fountains.
