utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: vision is for that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, um,

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, and so this is like, I guess, a multi-step planning process because you have RISE.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Absolutely, RISE.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And then you have like other things that are going to come out.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And how long do you envision this planning process to–

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: for this work product to be done.

chapters.summary: Prabilski says RISE will finish this year, procurement for the comprehensive plan starts next year, and the plan will take about two to three years. It will begin with visioning and listening to coastal communities and agencies.
chapters.title: Prabilski says comprehensive plan will take two to three years

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: The, right, RISE will be complete at the end of this year.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then there's building blocks and it's typology and really kind of breaking out the coastline.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then the comprehensive plan.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: New York State had a whole RISE program.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Wait, well, it's different.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank God.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, thank God.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then, so with the funding that we received this year, it includes funding to.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: both hire planners and procure consultants to support us in developing that plan.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So we should start procurement on the actual comprehensive plan next year.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then it'll take, I believe, I don't have the two years to complete the plan, maybe three.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay, so two or three years to do the whole plan.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And the first part of it will be a lot of that visioning, listening, understanding, building on rise, but visioning, listening, understanding with our coastal community and with our agencies and all the work that they're doing.

chapters.summary: Gennaro notes the Council created an Office of Long-Term Planning and Sustainability and an Office of Resiliency in the mayor's office. He asks how BCR works with that office.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks how BCR coordinates with Mayor's Office of Resiliency

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Here's a question.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, when I...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I, you know, the council created in the law the Office of Long-Term Planning and Sustainability and also created an Office of Resiliency in the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So we've got an office of resiliency just sitting over in the mayor's office, and I've got no one to blame but myself for creating it in law.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so they're over there.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You're over at Lefrak.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so how does that work?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: How do you work in...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Collaboration or whatever, because they're going to say, you know, like we're the original, you know, like we're the original, you know, resiliency person going back to like Dan Zerilli, you know, and so, so they're like thumping their chest saying like, we were here first.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says DEP has a strong working relationship with the mayor's resiliency office and there is no turf war. She thanks Gennaro for his advocacy for the Bureau's funding.
chapters.title: DeFalco says DEP works hand-in-glove with resiliency office

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think that we've had a terrific working relationship with that office.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And in all fairness, yes, we are in Queens, but, you know, we're often right here.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We've got an office across the street that I can see from here.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We work with, you know, them hand in glove, I think, on all of these projects.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I don't think that there is a turf war fight happening right now.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think there's too much work.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Okay, I'm just saying.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And there's plenty of work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Lots of people jumping in and a lot of expertise.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Even more coming based on the amount of staff that we're going to have coming with this $43 million.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And to that extent, we want to thank you because...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That's a lot of your advocacy for this bureau and for the way that this is set up, as I think this administration is listening.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This is funding that we've been working for for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And that you had supported for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So we thank you again for your advocacy on that.

chapters.summary: Gennaro says he has long viewed storm surge as the major threat and wants BCR to be the boss of coastal resiliency. He jokes about BCR becoming the 'Death Star' of resilience in a good way.
chapters.title: Gennaro discusses storm surge as primary risk and BCR's role

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, because I always wanted, you know, resiliency to, you know, proceed.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, back in.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Before I did that bill, now law, in 2012, I'm like, there's going to be, I didn't know its name was going to be Sandy, but this is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I've always, not that I'm poo-pooing sea level rise, but I always thought that storm surge is...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, is the big boogeyman and, you know, that could wipe us out tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Whereas, you know, Storm Love Arise, you know, I'm not going to live to see it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, I mean,

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: to that extent.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But, you know, it's huge.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, what we should do is in a measured, calculated way where everything is figured out in advance and how do we fund it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And now some of the pieces are, you know, coming together.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And I think this is the capstone on that to, you know, establish you folks as like, you know, the boss of coastal resiliency.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, everybody's got to come to you, talk to you, whatever.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It's a bad analogy, but...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I was looking at a Star Wars reference that doesn't quite fit here, so I'm not going to use it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But, you know, you...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay, okay, you guys are going to be like the Death Star of resilience, but in a good way, in a good Death Star, if you can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So they'll, you know, paint it blue or something like that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I said it.

chapters.summary: Gennaro reads DeFalco's testimony warning against fragmenting institutional structure and asks what in the bill triggered that concern. DeFalco says BCR is new, infrastructure is coming online, and the city needs flexibility and more conversation.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks DEP about fragmentation concerns in Intro 936

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And I want to, when you talk about the...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You make reference in the testimony, I'll read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: As the council considers the legislation, we think it is important to look closely at the institutional structure already built and make sure any changes strengthen the city's ability to deliver this work rather than inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Certainly fragmenting it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I just want to hear a little more about the basis of your fear about that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: There must be something in the bill that triggered you to say that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Triggered somebody to say it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: There it is, you know.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think that the larger point that we'd like to make about this, and

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This bureau was just started a couple years ago.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And when it was started, we didn't have infrastructure coming online in the same way that we do right now.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So, you know, it's one thing theoretically to think about operating floodgates.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's another thing to operate floodgates.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: You know, they're massive.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: How many shifts of people do you need?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're learning a lot as these things come online.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think you also see in the testimony that we said we'd like to have more conversations with you about this.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think that we want to be open-minded to what we're learning, what we're seeing from some of these studies,

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: and what this should look like in the future, and whether or not we should be thinking of any other sort of angles or ways to go about doing this and how it's set up, and to give ourselves some flexibility, I think, in the future to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, we're not against flexibility.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We're for that, and we're totally against fragmenting.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So, okay, fair enough.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks to what extent the Army Corps and HATS have embraced storm surge barriers and whether NYC could plan and deploy them. Prabilski says the Corps proposed barriers in reports but is not actively studying them.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about Army Corps storm surge barriers

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Here's another question out of nowhere.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Oh, am I holding you up?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You probably just have a couple things you want to say, right?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay, let me just do this one thing, and then I'm going to put you on, okay?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Then I'll go back.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I have more prepared questions.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But to what extent, and I should know more about this, but I don't, to what extent has the Army Corps and the HAT study

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: embraced storm surge barriers?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So there's their view of storm surge barriers.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And do you believe that your bureau and New York City as an entity has the ability to

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: plan for and deploy, you know, storm surge barrier technology, or is that kind of a bridge too far for our little town on the Hudson to, like, put that together and finance that?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We're talking big money here.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So first is, like, the vision of storm surge barriers by the Army Corps, and then...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Do what, you know, to what ability, you know, does our little town have the ability to do that on our own?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: If I do say so myself.

chapters.summary: Prabilski says the Corps has not advanced storm surge barrier analysis beyond reports and that the city needs Corps expertise to study, build, and operate them. Gennaro notes the barriers are on a map but not on the map as active projects.
chapters.title: Prabilski says storm surge barriers need more Corps study

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Yes, no.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: The storm surge barriers that the Army Corps proposed as part of HATS are significant, right, across Jamaica Bay.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: They're significant pieces of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: The Corps is not actively studying them, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: They're not moving forward on analyzing that.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I would say...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But they did advance them as projects, right?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: They have in other places.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: In the PAX study and in the original Jamaica Bay study, they proposed them at the mouth of Jamaica Bay as a means to protect against storm surge barriers.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Storm surge.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: But they have not advanced the study any further than that.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I believe right now the city does need the Corps and their expertise in that significant type of study of storm surge barriers to do that.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I believe within the city, yes, there is a lot of experts that could very much study that.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: But right now the Corps is not advancing it, and we really need their expertise on what it means for storm surge barrier, both to develop and build and to operate them.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay, so they're not really on the map right now, other than...

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: In a report.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Other than in a report, they're on a map.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And they were thought of as a good idea by the Corps, but, you know, they...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I guess they view the world through available resources and they make decisions.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: They need a lot more study, the barriers, yeah.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks if BCR has attended meetings of the Storm Surge Barrier Working Group associated with Malcolm Bowman. Prabilski says she is aware of the group but would need to check attendance.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about Storm Surge Barrier Working Group

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Are you aware of the Storm Surge Barrier Working Group or whatever, Malcolm Bowman and those guys?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I'm aware of the group, yes.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I think they're still meeting, you know.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Has anyone from the Bureau ever attended one of their meetings?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I would have to check with...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I used to be on it once when I was, you know, at DEC, but then, you know, I'm back here now.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Malcolm's a friend of mine, but I just...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And it's got this whole big working group, people from Columbia and stuff, but I don't know if they're...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You know, I don't know if a tree falls in the forest and, you know, like there's no one there.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It doesn't make a sound.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: They talk to themselves, but I don't know how much they get around.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And with that, it is my distinct pleasure to recognize Councilmember Avila for questions for as long as she wants to ask them.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Avilés thanks the panel and says Red Hook residents were surprised by the Bureau's creation. She asks how BCR will engage impacted communities and how it will plan its work.
chapters.title: Avilés asks about community engagement for new Bureau

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: He really likes me.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: You bet.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you so much for being here.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Avilés thanks the panel and says Red Hook residents were surprised by the Bureau's creation. She asks how BCR will engage impacted communities and how it will plan its work.
chapters.title: Avilés asks about community engagement for new Bureau

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I wanted just to follow up on a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of the, I think many folks in Red Hook Your Home community,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We're really happy to hear about this announcement of the creation, and then we're also mystified that they had no idea any of this was coming together.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I'd love to know what is going to be the planned community engagement around how we call it the Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: What should we call it?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: The Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Will plan its work moving forward?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think, I mean, you were talking about like what community engagement in terms of like RISE and other reports that we're working on.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Or how this bureau is going to, like what is the vision for the bureau and how does the bureau plan to engage those impacted communities?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Because I will say folks were very surprised to even hear of its creation.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Delighted because as an impacted community, this is, and dealing with the construction of the resiliency project right now and knowing that that project.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Is built for a 10-year flood, not a 100-year, and it's going to be inadequate before we get to the big kahuna anyway.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So this is going to be an ongoing issue for this community that was flooded this weekend.

chapters.summary: DeFalco says the Red Hook project involved community input on flood wall height and that thinking about coastal versus inland flooding has evolved. She says BCR will be a big part of future community engagement.
chapters.title: DeFalco describes Red Hook engagement and evolving resilience thinking

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think especially, and the Red Hook Coastal Resiliency Project is a good example of, I think, how things are evolving.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: At the time that the project was being looked at and designed, the community was very concerned about the height of flood walls.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And some of the reasons things were designed the way that they were designed and the level of protection that they were designed at was directly from community engagement and community input.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Oh, not the limitations of FEMA?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Because I was told that much of that, like in one section, there's a wall this big.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: That that was FEMA limitations and FEMA design.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Obviously, this has been going on for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: The community engagement becomes important.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think the Bureau of Coastal Resiliency is incredibly important because we can see even in just the last few years how our thought process about what protection means has evolved.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And especially, I mean, even in just the time that I've been at DEP, the amount of rainstorms and the way that we're thinking about inland flooding versus coastal flooding and how they're intersecting has changed, I think, pretty dramatically in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And so thinking about what we do to supplement projects down the road is going to be a big part of that community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: My bureau is going to be very part of that, a big part of that community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We work very closely together.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're working together now on different studies that are happening out in Jamaica Bay and Springfield Creek on how we are engaging communities, especially in areas where there may or may not be buyouts needed and how that intersects with the projects that are being

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: planned there, even if they're federal projects or federally funded projects.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So that's a thing that we're coming up with.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Also, with the additional money that the administration has put forward, we're going to have a lot more capacity to be able, I think, to do more community outreach.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: There's no question that we would like to be doing a lot more than we've been able to do.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And we're also looking at the way that we do community outreach, I think, very differently.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: A big part of what my bureau used to do was a lot of proactive community outreach.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And right now, given the amount of storms and, right, the amount of, like, everybody's calling us with a clogged catch basin.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But when you have a storm, 25% of the time we're in a flash flood warning or more this year.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That really changes, like, people, we were doing proactive community engagement, and I feel like sometimes now we're doing more case management.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And so we've got to think about how we staff and work together on this vision to be able to improve the community engagement, something we're definitely thinking about and want to work on.

chapters.summary: Avilés says residents want real engagement and describes having to call agencies to remove catch basin covers before storms. She asks for automatic procedures and contractor accountability.
chapters.title: Avilés raises coordination problems with catch basins and flooding

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think the continued request that I hear is just the community really wanting to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And real challenges of coordination.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Like we actually had to call people to tell them to remove one city agency, cover the catch basins with those plastic things, and then we have to call the agency to say, there's a lot of rain coming, we're going to flood,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: can you remove that?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Can we figure out a way how that should be an automatic, like, there's a storm, you cover the catch basins in a community that floods, you should remove that and not wait for the council member to call staff.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that that's definitely something that we're working on, especially also like a lot of that involves contractors, right?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And so that's been one of the really big challenges in figuring out how we manage that and work with other agencies to manage that on a more frequent basis.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It didn't, we weren't trying to cover it, trying to cover them so people don't pour concrete and other things down them.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And now you're uncovering them and covering them and uncovering them.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And it's been nonstop.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So the way that we staff and think about how we're staffing our community relations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: unit and how that's intersecting with our Bureau of Coastal Resilience, I think is going to be a big part of it.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Some of the reason that we're doing those flooding town halls is that sometimes is the way that we can proactively talk to people in a community about what's happening or give them the opportunity to come out and meet with our experts.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And so we're trying to be a little more creative about how we do that in different communities, but we'd like to be doing a lot more of it than we're doing, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And y'all have done some really great work.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I know it is a challenge cutting across multiple agencies.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: many, many contractors.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And so I don't know if that's something that's embedded just as a matter of practice.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Like when there is an emergency, you uncover these things as a matter of practice in a contract.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And if you don't, and the city incurs costs because of the flooding as a result of that, then maybe you should take

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: that hit as opposed to us constantly paying for inadequate contractors who are doing things they shouldn't be doing.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: But in terms of the office just generally, I think my statement here really is our community would very much like to be engaged on this issue as we are experiencing a resiliency project, which is very unique compared to all the others.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: The cheapest of the group, but also weaving in and out of private property.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And many community members are feeling like it's also a pretty inadequate project for the peninsula itself.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I think there's a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: to be done and a lot of concern and concern around the city's what they call economic development but is simply putting more housing in areas that flood so

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: how how is the agency engaged in these conversations because there seems to be not a lot of coherence

chapters.summary: DeFalco says DEP is engaged in development conversations and points to the unified stormwater rule and Gowanus as positive examples. She acknowledges the need to avoid creating a bathtub effect when building coastal protection.
chapters.title: DeFalco responds on development, stormwater rules, and bathtub effect

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're very engaged in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: And as you can imagine, I'm especially interested in how it is that we are developing and also making sure that we have capacity for it.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think that there's good news that comes with development.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We've talked about the unified stormwater rule requiring people to manage more stormwater on their property.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So that's the thing that becomes beneficial as you see development.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We're seeing that positively in Gowanus where different properties that weren't managing stormwater are now managing stormwater because they've been developed.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But when you're talking about something like BMT, it...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: it's going to intersect with the existing infrastructure at the same time that you're building more coastal resilience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So I think that...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Well, for those residents, you're not building it for the other residents because it protects them.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We are and will.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's a thing that you're going to see, and I think that we're working very, very hard on what it means for the inland or sort of, you know, I think we're talking about the bathtub effect, right?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: How we're making sure that the existing properties are taken care of.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That we're not creating a problem by trying to address another problem.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I think everyone has identified that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We have not seen any response to that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Or a commitment to investing in the infrastructure that would make sure that that is prevented.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So, like, it's an acknowledged challenge, but I don't see any agency actually responding in concrete terms to that impact.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I think obviously these are long, ongoing conversations.

chapters.summary: Avilés asks whether outside teams or trained community members will deploy barriers. Prabilski says BCR will house its own crews, hired through DEP's apprentice program, to deploy gates and barriers.
chapters.title: Avilés asks how flood barriers will be deployed during storms

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I think the other thing I just wanted to ask in terms of the resiliency projects that depend on, you know, deploying the barriers and stuff and as you hire up,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: is the intention that there will be a team from outside that comes in during storms to deploy these barriers?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Or is there any thinking about training teams or people of communities that can actually do these that are closer to?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: To the barriers themselves.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So the crews that will be deploying the barriers will be a crew housed within BCR.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We've started hiring up through the cities, hiring, right now they're hiring through an apprentice program within DEP.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: There's still a number of postings to go, kind of hiring those crews to be brought up to speed over the next year, year and a half on the coastal defense system that includes the walls and

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: gates and barriers on the east side of Manhattan and then in the ones in Red Hook.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Yeah, so it is, it are outside crews in as much as they're hired by DEP and they will come to the neighborhoods and deploy those gates.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: But then how,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, how you cover such a geographically vast and in some ways transportationally challenged, particularly in a storm area, is a creative element I can't quite wrap my brain around.

chapters.summary: Avilés asks how development, industrial working waterfront, maritime uses, housing, and coastal resiliency will be reconciled. Prabilski says it will be a challenge and BCR will need to bring all voices together.
chapters.title: Avilés presses on development and industrial waterfront in coastal vision

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: The last question, in terms of the overall vision for coastal resiliency, how...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: How does development factor into how these plans are being visioned and engaged?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And also as a council member that has a very large industrial manufacturing working waterfront,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'm seeing the tensions and contradictions of kind of an incoherent policy model around economic development, industrial working waterfront, maritime, housing.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And coastal resiliency.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So how does that factor into the vision and the management across multiple agencies?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I think it'll be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We can agree.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I think it'll be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: You know, one of the first parts as well is I think we've also mentioned the

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: some additional visioning and we want to embrace the

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: voices and the visions of those different players.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: As Beth said, you know, developers have a role to play within the city's infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And the working maritime also has an important, important role to play.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And so we really will have to work with those neighborhood communities, the folks that live there, the folks that work there.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We're just now getting started.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We don't have a...

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: A vision of what the answer is yet, right?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Because we need to develop it.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So we really will want to get all of those voices together.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And the need for green space, the desire for green space and access to the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: There are trade-offs with coastal protection.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We can have a large 10-foot wall, but you can't access your waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: But New York City is a city of their neighborhoods that want to be on their waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And so we have to balance all those things.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I guess my final plug will be as, again, a representative of an industrial manufacturing waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: That has been utterly disincentivized to use the water when we as a city need to learn how to be with the water because it is not going anywhere, it's just getting higher.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: You know, I would really encourage

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: us to push integration of economic development, integrating into the use of the water and not just hard lining every edge so that we can look at it as pretty or

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: to build luxury condos on the water.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Like those feel like where we're headed without the others.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I just want to encourage some deep caution and skepticism on my behalf, but it is really, if we cannot build a resilient city without economic development that is integrated into using the water

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: and getting us to move things on the water.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gennaro thanks Avilés, calls her an honorary committee member, and resumes his questions. He then turns to the Plan YC process.
chapters.title: Gennaro thanks Avilés and resumes questioning

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: You're an honorary member of the committee now.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It's not legal, but, you know, honorary.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks how BCR will interact with the Plan YC process, which also includes resiliency work. Prabilski says DEP works closely with MOCEJ on Plan YC and BCR was established from a Plan YC initiative.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks how BCR interacts with Plan YC

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, before I get to the repair question, just something just popped into my head.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Now, the...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: The Plan YC process.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That's kind of its own thing.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: How do you envision BCR kind of,

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: you know, interacting with the whole Plan YC process because there are some, you know, there's resiliency stuff that comes out of that too.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so what are your thoughts on that?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: We work very closely with MOC EJ and the development and updates of Plan YC, we being DEP and all the rest of the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I think you could say that the Plan YC and the development of the updates is a collaborative process across the agencies and we'll continue to participate in that.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I mean, I think that's kind of the easiest.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I mean, the Bureau of Creation was established from a Plan YC initiative.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then where Coastal lives within Plan YC, you know, we're kind of following and tracking those goals or pushing on those goals as well.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm always just like looking for like little tripwires about how...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, everyone's all for, you know, cooperation and stuff like that, but I...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Something to think about that, you know, because you got, you know, you have your own internal planning process and then Plan YC comes along and they got another idea.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so feel free to come to me.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I'll break the tie if there's any kind of major clash between you and MLC EJ.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks if the nor'easter required mobile flood barriers or subway entrance covers. DeFalco says it did not; the storm was mostly coastal and tidal flooding, and pumping had to wait for tides to recede.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks whether weekend storm required resiliency deployments

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Here's from the prepared questions.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Did this past weekend storm require the deployment of any resiliency strategies put in place since Sandy?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: For example, things like mobile flood barriers and subway station entrance covers.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: If so, which strategies were deployed and how did they fare?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This weekend's storm didn't require that.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Subway stations, we mostly saw it was coastal and tidal flooding, not inland flooding as much.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So the difficult part with the coastal flooding is that it's...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Until the tide goes down, you can't start pumping.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Otherwise, it just fills right back up.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's like pumping the ocean.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So we know the areas that were likely to get hit.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: This storm really sat over the city for days, and especially with the full moon, that didn't help things in a nor'easter.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So really for us, it was just...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: making sure that we were clearing areas that we could and pumping low-lying areas once the tide had gone down.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: That was the chief responsibility.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks about rainfall totals and notes his central Queens district missed the worst. DeFalco says rainfall was relatively light and inland flooding reports were minimal.
chapters.title: Gennaro and DeFalco discuss weekend rainfall and inland flooding

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Do you focus on how much rain we got during this thing?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I would have to double check on the exact precipitation.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It was pretty slow, relatively light.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: We didn't see a lot of reports of inland flooding.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It was really just the coastal areas that we expected.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, because my part of Queens, I'm like Central Queens.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I'm like Central Eastern Queens.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And, you know, it's like we missed out on the nor'easter.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We had some breezes, didn't really get super heavy rain.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I live in Jamaica Estates, which has like huge trees, and I just thought we were going to be a goner.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And I think one tree fell down in the entirety of the estates.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, and so I, but I, you know, all the reports about the coast getting beat up, that was hard to process.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks if BCR has filled its 69 new lines. DeFalco says not yet, but hiring of apprentice laborers and other roles is underway, with a goal to fill positions as soon as possible.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about filling 69 new BCR positions

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Has the Bureau filled its 69 new lines?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: If not, how many of those positions are filled to date?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: No, we haven't filled all 69 yet.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I believe that we have already started hiring some of the apprentice laborers and getting them onboarded and are continuing to aggressively work on that hiring process.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, let's talk about these lines.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: These are for...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: People in the field doing labor stuff?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Many of them are, but I mean, there are a lot of different types of jobs that will be involved in that.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: You're going to have planning and engineers as well.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But I think, you know, a good opportunity for people to do and become apprentice laborers that then turn into laborers and are able to move, you know, up in the system through that experience.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: But, yeah, you'll have all types of levels.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think right now what we are trying to make sure is that we've got enough people to be able to operate.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Gates, as they come online, and they're coming online, you know, more and more quickly in the next year.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay, and so what's like the timeline for the...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Filling of the new lines, do you think?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Yeah, I think they're trying to fill everything by next year.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Next year meaning the beginning of next year, the end of next year, or, you know?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: Literally as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: It's a full...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: It didn't help me, though.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I don't know that we've gotten exact.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Does anyone be giving you a hard time?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: OMB would never give us a hard time.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: No, it's not that.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I think you're just looking at the sheer volume of trying to hire that many people all at once and trying to get through that.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So you're going from...

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: A bureau of six people to 75.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: So, you know, we're moving as fast as humanly possible.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Like, do you have a place for them?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I mean, you guys are in the regular left rack, right?

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco
utterances.text: I mean, we've got facilities all over the city.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Yeah, you guys are all over.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks whether DEP has worked with MOCEJ on climate resiliency guidelines and the minimum resilience score required by Local Law 41. Prabilski says MOCEJ leads the effort and DEP coordinates with them.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about Local Law 41 resiliency score rulemaking

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: In accordance with Local Law 41 of 2021, MOCEJ

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: published climate resiliency guidelines for the design and construction of covered capital projects.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That local law also requires MOC-EJ in consultation with other agencies to promulgate rules by December 31st of this year to establish a minimum resilience score

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: by which covered projects must be measured.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Have you worked with MOCEJ on the resiliency score metric?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Have you consulted with them about their upcoming rulemaking?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That is rulemaking on local of what?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: They didn't do the rulemaking for local of 41 yet?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Oh, so Local 041 is like successive rounds of rulemaking.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, but do you?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Well, I can give you an answer on a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: How about that?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: MOCEJ is leading on the CRDG, the Climate Resilience Design Guidelines, enactment for the local law requirements.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: They're coordinating across all agencies and particularly within DEP for some of those resilience goals.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So, yes, we...

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: The agency coordinates with MOCEJ as they're leading on completing that requirement from the local law.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks if BCR is coordinating with DOB on the waterfront construction code. Prabilski says she sits on a committee for the code and sees it as helpful for consistency, with no immediate major concerns.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about waterfront construction code coordination

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Is the Bureau coordinating with DOB on the creation of its waterfronts construction code?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: What are the Bureau's primary concerns or goals relating to such code?

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I sit on the committee, one of the committees for the Waterfront Code.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And there's one or two other folks from DEP as well.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: And then folks across all agencies and experts and consultants across the city.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So, yes, in short, we do coordinate with DOB on the Waterfront Code development.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I don't have an immediate, like, big concern with the code.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: I think it'll be really great for consistency in how we build on the waterfront since there was a little bit crossing jurisdictions previously.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: So I think it'll be, I think, and throughout the work that they've been leading, it's been really...

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Interesting to see those shared conversations, trying to tease out what makes it difficult and unclear in regards to building on the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Both, yeah, so I don't see any big risks right now.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Catherine Prabilski
utterances.text: Trying to be optimistic.

chapters.summary: Gennaro asks how codifying BCR within DEP would affect its ability to advocate for resources. DeFalco says DEP wants flexibility and time to see how the expanded bureau operates before supporting codification.
chapters.title: Gennaro asks about codifying BCR within DEP versus separate department

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: If this bill, meaning the one we're hearing today, were to codify the Bureau within DEP rather than establishing a separate department, how would...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: In that effect, the Bureau's ability to advocate for resources or achieve its work.

utterances.speaker: Beth DeFalco

chapters.summary: Kilkenny says New Yorkers remain at risk from storm surge and Riverkeeper opposes creating a new department. She urges amending Intro 936 to codify BCR within DEP to preserve expertise, job pipeline, and recent $43 million investment.
chapters.title: Brianna Kilkenny testifies for Riverkeeper on Intro 936

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: My name is Brianna Kilkenny, and I am the New York City Advocacy and Policy Intern at Riverkeeper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairperson Gennaro and members of the committee for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Riverkeeper is a member-supported watchdog organization dedicated to protecting and restoring the Hudson River and the waters of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Most New Yorkers today are as at risk from coastal storm surge as they were 14 years ago when Superstorm Sandy hit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: And the storm this past weekend was a clear example of this, with high tide and storm surge flooding inundating communities across Queens, Brooklyn, and Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: It is clear that action needs to be taken, and Riverkeeper applauds the Council for taking leadership on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: While we support the intent behind Intro 936, we join our partners in the Rise to Resilience Coalition in our opposition to the creation of a new department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Currently, the Bureau of Coastal Resilience resides within the DEP, and this has allowed the Bureau to benefit greatly from DEP's expertise in operating and maintaining large infrastructure,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: as well as benefiting from DEP's job training pipeline and existing personnel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: If the Bureau were to be made into its own department, it is likely that both of these benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: would be lost, which could increase costs and timelines for new projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Riverkeeper was very glad to see Mayor Mondani's administration make a historic $43 million investment into the Bureau this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: With this new funding, increased alignment within the administration, and dedication to pursue a much-needed citywide coastal resilience plan, Riverkeeper strongly requests that the Council maintain a Bureau of Coastal Resilience within DEP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: Until 936 should be amended to codify a Bureau of Coastal Resilience within the DEP to ensure that progress and benefits that have been made over the last several years are not erased by a future administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: If amended as such, Riverkeeper would strongly support the bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna Kilkenny
utterances.text: So thank you, Chairman Gennaro, for the opportunity to testify today, and we look forward to working with you on this legislation in the future.

chapters.summary: Villatoro says climate change amplifies environmental injustice and supports the $43 million BCR investment. She supports Intro 936 intent but wants BCR permanently within DEP, supports Intro 931 with a cost-benefit analysis, and urges funding for MOCEJ and DEP.
chapters.title: Katelyn Villatoro testifies for NYLCV on climate adaptation and bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Caitlin Vietoro, and I'm the New York City Policy Fellow at the New York League of Conservation Voters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Gennaro and members of the Committee on Environmental Protection for the opportunity to testify, and we will be submitting longer testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: New Yorkers face increasingly frequent and severe rainfall, coastal flooding, storm surge, groundwater flooding, and sea level rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: Climate change also amplifies the impacts of environmental injustice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: Pre-existing socioeconomic challenges combined with disproportionate climate change impacts leave low-income and communities of color more vulnerable than others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: And we appreciate the leadership of the City Council on investments reaching these communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: We also strongly support the Mamdani administration's FY27 investment in the Bureau of Coastal Resilience to establish critical in-house capacity to manage the city's growing portfolio of shoreline protection assets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: As a member of the Rise to Resilience Coalition, we strongly supported Local Law 122 of 2021, establishing a five-borough climate adaptation plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: We had hoped to see more progress on this plan by now, but we look forward to working with MOCEJ to develop a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: and equitable and long-term climate adaptation plan in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: This plan should work off of previous neighborhood-led plans and include recommendations to protect residents, property, and infrastructure throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: It should identify climate vulnerable areas to determine where adaptation measures should first be implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: Lastly, NYLCV strongly supports allocating more funding for MOCEJ and DEP staffing and long-term funding for capital projects concerning coastal resilience, green infrastructure, cloudburst management, and blue belt programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: And regarding today's bills, we appreciate the intent of Intro 936.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: However, we believe a Bureau of Coastal Resilience should be permanently established within the DEP, especially given the funding already taking place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: We recommend a cost-benefit analysis be conducted to compare costs of a mobile drinking fleet with increased permanent water fountains throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katelyn Villatoro
utterances.text: And we look forward to working with the Council and Mumdani administration to prepare for the risks of climate change.

chapters.summary: Elizabeth Cortez, an MPH student, supports Intro 931 with a funded implementation plan. She cites heat mortality disparities and urges recurring summer service, priority for vulnerable neighborhoods, and annual public reporting.
chapters.title: Elizabeth Cortez testifies on Intro 931 mobile drinking fountains

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gennaro and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: My name is Elizabeth Cortez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: I am an MPH student at Kinesi SPH, speaking in my personal capacity as a New York City resident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: I support advancing Intro 931 with a feasible implementation plan and adequate resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: The Health Department's 2026 NYC Heat-Related Mortality Report shows that heat stress death rates are higher among Black and Latino New Yorkers and in lower-income neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: As the committee works through staffing and costs, I urge it to preserve the bill's recurring summer service and a priority for high-vulnerability neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Heat risks also extend beyond declared emergencies, which supports the bill's approach of providing drinking water on hot days throughout the summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Fountains cannot replace cooling or address every source of heat risk, but making drinking water easier to access in public spaces is a practical complement to cooling in neighborhoods most vulnerable to heat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: The DEP's earlier water on the go mobile drinking fountain experience offers lessons, but today's testimony makes it clear that expansion would require substantial

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: new capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Therefore, I urge the committee to work with DEP and other relevant agencies on a funded implementation plan that protects core water and emergency services, including consideration of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: appropriate lead agency and existing staff sites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: I also recommend annual public reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Neighborhood coverage, operating hours and costs so the council can assess whether the program reaches high vulnerability neighborhoods and how resources are being used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Cortez
utterances.text: Thank you for considering my testimony.

summary: Committee on Environmental Protection and Waterfronts holds an oversight hearing on coastal resilience and Intros 343, 931, and 936.
